title: Separating Ideal-Circuit Structure from Hardware-Dependent Deviations in a Fixed 35-Qubit Diagnostic Circuit on IBM Heron Processors
abstract: H. Billah and M.M.H. Sarker contributed equally to this work. Interpreting a fixed quantum circuit's output as evidence of a hardware effect requires ruling out two things usually conflated with it: finite-sample fluctuation, and structure already present in the circuit's own noiseless output. Less commonly checked is a third: whether the reference circuit compared against is the one actually executed, once compiler-level qubit routing is accounted for. We execute a fixed 35-qubit, 243-gate diagnostic circuit on IBM Heron-family hardware (three runs, two backends) and show this third check is essential: the routed circuit submitted to hardware has different noiseless predictions than the logical circuit intended, for several qubits. Against the correct, routed-circuit reference, the aggregate deviation is significant in two of three runs, and four registers (0, 9, 14, 27) show a significant output-probability deviation in every run — though we distinguish a high-confidence subset, {0, 9, 27}, with tightly time-matched calibration, from qubit 14, included only on an exploratory basis given its calibration was retrieved roughly two weeks post-execution. Same-backend replicates correlate more strongly by the Pearson measure, though a rank-based (Spearman) test shows this gap does not survive at the level of register ordering, indicating substantial leverage from a small number of registers rather than a broadly robust pattern; these three executions also share a byte-identical payload and are not independent replications in the strictest sense. The mechanism is only partially resolved: independent single-qubit readout error and raw gate count are ruled out as complete explanations for most of these registers, but the simplest version of the leading hypothesis for the single most-affected register does not reproduce the observed cross-backend pattern even with live, backend-specific timing data. A second, structurally different circuit validated only in simulation calibrates the statistical procedure's behavior under one synthetic noise model; it does not itself establish generality to real hardware, and the specific register set found here should not be expected to generalize beyond this study. Note on scope: this is a methodology and case-study contribution centered on executed-circuit references for fixed-circuit diagnostics, not a characterization of IBM Heron hardware in general or a randomized-benchmarking experiment in the formal sense. Supporting data, the routed OpenQASM circuits, raw measurement counts, and analysis code for this study are available on request from the corresponding author. Affiliation: Sonicium Quantum Lab Ltd., Dhaka, Bangladesh.

title: A Transformer-Based Framework for Offensive Language Detection in Kannada-English Code-Mixed Text
abstract: This paper explores the usefulness of multilingual transformer-based models in the detection of offensive language on Kannada-English code-mixed social media text. This work compares CNNTFIDF, XLMR, IndicBERT, and DistilBERT models, and suggests a better DistilBERT-related model using specific preprocessing and fine-tuning to low-resource code-mixed text. The experiments carried out using a trained Kannada-English dataset show that the proposed DistilBERT model has an F1-score of 0.846 and an accuracy of 85.93, which is better than heavier multilingual transformers and is computationally efficient. The findings point to the appropriateness of lightweight transformer architectures in detecting offensive language using low-resource and code-mixed languages. The work offers empirical information and baselines to be used in the creation of scalable and inclusive multilingual online community content moderation systems.

title: Constraint-Augmented Transformer Architectures for Generating Shakespearean Sonnets and Dramatic Verse
abstract: This study explores the effectiveness of constraint-augmented neural networks for generating Shakespearean sonnets and dramatic verse, with a focus on incorporating formal prosodic constraints into transformer models. Using a corpus of canonical Shakespearean texts, a multi-stage methodology was employed: corpus normalisation, meter- and rhyme-sensitive tokenisation, transformer fine-tuning and constraint-aware decoding via penalty-regularised beam search. Perplexity was used for fluency and Distinct-n for lexical diversity, while human ratings were used for stylistic authenticity, emotional resonance and semantic coherence. Results show constraint-augmented models reduced perplexity by 38% compared to LSTM baselines and achieved significant gains in lexical diversity and stylistic alignment. Human evaluators rated constraint-aware outputs as more authentic and affectively salient, so constraint-aware models preserve both formal fidelity and expressive depth.

title: Structural Cryptanalysis of a Graph-Based Adjacency-Matrix Transformation Derived from the Middle Graph of a Star Graph
abstract: This paper provides a structural cryptanalysis of a graph-based matrix transformation obtained from the normalized adjacency matrix of the middle graph of a star. The construction is specified with canonical indexed vertices and edges, exact rational arithmetic, a deterministic auxiliary sequence, and an invertible integer key matrix. For every valid block of length n, the graph matrix has rank 2n rather than 2n+1. This invariant row dependence survives right multiplication by the secret matrix: a single ciphertext reveals all auxiliary values yi and n complete rows of the key. If the same key matrix is reused for two known plaintext/ciphertext pairs whose recovered y-vectors differ, the complete matrix key is uniquely recovered from a stacked linear system. A seeded numerical experiment confirms this recovery over multiple block lengths. We further show that fuzzy normalization is only public reversible scaling and therefore adds no cryptographic hiding. The results establish the construction as a reproducible negative case study in graph-based cryptography rather than a stand-alone secure cipher.

title: PLCWorld: Benchmarking LLM-Generated PLC Programs in Closed-Loop Plant Simulation
abstract: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs) coordinate industrial equipment by reading sensor inputs and issuing control commands. Evaluating whether large language model (LLM)-generated PLC programs satisfy task requirements and safety constraints requires observing how their commands affect device and workpiece states. We introduce PLCWorld, a common closed-loop execution environment and benchmark that couples Structured Text (ST) execution with simulated plant responses and sensor feedback. Grounded in control relations identified in industrial PLC programs and engineering documentation, PLCWorld contains 100 synthetic tasks and 473 registered task-condition pairs across Motion Control and Material Handling, with difficulty defined by control-dependency scope. A common protocol reports Task Success and Safety Violation separately. Validation combines practitioner review, reference and alternative programs, targeted counterexamples, specification-evaluator alignment checks, and comparisons with independent ST runtimes. Reference and alternative programs satisfy their applicable cases, while all 542 targeted counterexamples activate their designated evaluator rules under at least one registered condition. Execution Gap relates submission-profile acceptance to subsequent task failure or observed Safety Violation. Across the constructed task groups, direct GPT-5.5 achieves 82.70% Task Success on Easy cases but 25.10% on Hard cases. Evaluations of six LLMs and four adapted generation-and-verification workflows further expose differences between completion, safety, and generation cost. Our code, simulation environment, benchmark tasks, and baseline implementations are publicly available at https://yunji0516.github.io/PLCWorld/.

title: Root-sparsity scaling for Hamiltonian simulation, differential equations and linear-system solvers
abstract: We give quantum algorithms for Hamiltonian simulation, linear differential equations, and linear systems with square-root dependence on sparsity. For an $s$-sparse Hermitian matrix with row and column Euclidean norms bounded by $η$, evolution for time $t$ to error $ε$ uses $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{s}τ+\sqrt{sτ\log(1/ε)}+\log(1/ε))$ queries, where $τ=η|t|$. The same bound holds for time-dependent Hamiltonians with coherent time-indexed sparse access and certified time discretisation. Our construction combines an exact entrywise representation with Cayley transducers. A joint lower bound nearly matches the time, sparsity, and precision dependence, ruling out a uniformly additive bound in $\sqrt{s}τ$ and $\log(1/ε)$. For dissipative linear differential equations we obtain $\mathcal{O}(\bar g[\sqrt{s}(τ+\sqrtτ)+1]\log(C\bar g/ε))$ queries, where $τ$ is the evolution time multiplied by a norm bound, $\bar g$ bounds the ratio of combined input and source norms to the final-solution norm, and $C$ is an absolute constant. We sharpen this bound by separating Hamiltonian and dissipative components, and treat general constant generators. Lower bounds capture joint parameter dependence for time-dependent equations and precision hardness for constant positive semidefinite dissipation. For linear systems, a Cayley walk and Chebyshev filter give $\mathcal{O}(κ\sqrt{s}\log(1/ε))$ queries when $\|A\|\le1$ and $\|A^{-1}\|\leκ$, and we give an alternative proof of a matching joint lower bound. We also give gate-efficient implementations of time-independent Hamiltonian simulation and the dissipative ODE solver, including Lipschitz time dependence, retaining the query bounds with polylogarithmic overhead in inverse precision given efficient entry decoding, arithmetic, and required source preparations.

title: An Omnilingual-ASR-Based Speech-LLM System for the 2nd MLC-SLM Challenge
abstract: We describe our submission to Task 1 of the 2nd MLC-SLM Challenge: a cascaded diarization-then-recognition system that combines DiariZen-Large-s80 (WavLM-Large) segmentation, CAM++ embedding-based two-speaker clustering, and a LoRA-adapted omniASR LLM 7B v2 recognizer, with no oracle segmentation or speaker labels at test time.On the official Development set (150 conversations, 21 language/accent categories) the system attains a macro tcpMER of 29.27%, versus 79.15% for the official baseline; on the Evaluation set it scores 50.23%.We also analyze two engineering choices that substantially affect tcpMER.First, embedding-based speaker clustering outperforms an end-to-end-style alternative that assigns speakers from ASR turn markers alone.Second, overlap-aware segmentation, although intended to raise diarization recall, increases tcpMER because overlapped speech is transcribed twice.

title: P052: Enterprise RAG over governed data: Microsoft Azure study
abstract: Enterprise RAG over governed data: Microsoft Azure study Author: Sonu Kumar Singh (Senior Consultant — Cloud & AI Solutions Architecture, Capgemini US LLC) Professional Credential: Member, IEEE (Membership # 102728576) | ORCID: 0009-0002-9180-4946 Abstract Enterprise generative AI becomes dependable only when retrieval, tools, identity, policy, provenance, evaluation, and human oversight are engineered as a system around the model. Against this backdrop, the paper examines enterprise RAG over governed data in Microsoft Azure. It asks a focused question: How should enterprise RAG over governed data be designed, governed, and empirically evaluated for Microsoft Azure? Here, the topic is treated as a set of engineering obligations, not a slogan. The important questions are what must remain correct under scale and failure, which controls must follow the workload across services, and which measurements would be needed to support a claim. Framing the topic this way prevents the analysis from reducing to a list of vendor capabilities. The main contribution is a structured way to move from architectural claims to evidence. Using controlled benchmark and statistical evaluation, the paper links design choices with security controls, operating assumptions, economics, and reproducibility. It does not fill gaps with synthetic benchmark numbers; instead, it defines the experiment that would be required to turn a design hypothesis into a supported result. Architectural Research Scope Research Domain / Theme: Generative AI & Agentic Systems Architectural Scope: Microsoft Azure Core Research Question: How should enterprise rag over governed data be designed, governed, and empirically evaluated for Microsoft Azure? Specification Standard: Full 20-page peer-level monograph featuring system topology diagrams, 7 empirical benchmark tables, and failure-mode analyses. Published as part of the Cloud, AI, and Distributed Data Systems: 500-Monograph Engineering Corpus.

title: privacy-flow: deterministic static analysis of personal-data flows
abstract: piiflow finds where personal data goes in a codebase — logs, third-party SDKs, LLM providers and outbound HTTP — and reports each path as a cited chain of file:line hops, with SARIF, canonical JSON flow facts and Fides egress declarations. It is deterministic and offline and calls no model. This archive holds the tool, its rule catalogue, the flow-facts and configuration JSON Schemas, and the conformance corpus (conformance/): small programs with hand-written expected flows and an external-runner contract for scoring any analyser.
